summary: This unit teaches you to give a safe, hygienic paraffin wax treatment to the hands and feet: consult the client and check for contraindications, set up and test the paraffin bath, apply the wax by the dip, brush or liner method, wrap and time the treatment, remove the wax, and deal with any reaction. You will also learn where the treatment fits into a manicure or pedicure, how to look after the bath safely, and what aftercare advice and records to give.

blocks.p: A paraffin wax treatment wraps the hands or feet in warm, soft wax. The warmth increases the blood flow, softens the skin and cuticles, helps creams soak in and eases stiff joints. It is a popular extra with a manicure or pedicure, and clients with dry, hard-working hands or aching joints feel the benefit at once.

Warm wax, a heated bath, a shared product and a client who may not feel heat well: this is a treatment where **heat safety and hygiene** matter at every step. This unit teaches you the method, but it also teaches you when not to go ahead and what to do if something goes wrong.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks in the Centre's salon. In the practical tasks you give a paraffin hand treatment by the dip method and a paraffin foot treatment by the brush or liner method, each with a consultation, a wrist test, correct wrapping and timing, and a clean, safe station at the end. The assessor watches your checks and your safety as closely as the treatment itself.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: What paraffin wax is and what it does

ul: **Paraffin wax** is a soft, white or colourless wax made from **petroleum** (crude oil). It is solid at room temperature and melts at a low heat.

Wax sold for beauty use often has added oils (for example mineral oil) and sometimes scent or colour, to make it softer, more moisturising and more pleasant. Plain, unscented wax is kept for clients who are sensitive to perfume.
The wax **sets (goes hard) as it cools**. On the skin it forms a close-fitting coat that holds in heat.

Working temperature: most paraffin baths hold the wax at about **50 to 55 °C**, as the maker sets. That is warm enough to stay liquid but, with care, not hot enough to burn. The exact setting is the maker's: follow the bath's instructions.
Paraffin is **flammable**. It will not catch fire at bath temperature, but if it is overheated, for example in a pot on a stove, it can smoke and burst into flames.

flow: Warm liquid wax is applied in several thin layers
It sets into a warm, close-fitting coat
The coat holds in the heat and traps the skin's moisture and any cream beneath it
The warmth increases the blood flow to the skin
Hard skin and cuticles soften; joints feel eased
The wax is removed and the cream is massaged in

head: Benefit
Why it happens
rows: Softer, moisturised skin
The sealed coat stops water escaping from the skin and helps the cream soak in.
Softer cuticles and hard skin
Warmth and moisture soften keratin.
Better blood flow; warm, pink skin
Heat widens the small blood vessels in the dermis.
Relief for stiff, aching joints
Deep, moist heat relaxes the muscles and eases stiffness. Many people with arthritis use it at home.
Relaxation
The warmth is soothing, and the treatment includes a massage.

ul: Clients with dry, rough, cracked or hard-working hands: from washing clothes by hand, cleaning, farming, gardening, hairdressing or working with cement.
Clients with dry, cracked heels and hard skin on the feet.
Clients with stiff, aching joints from arthritis, once their doctor agrees.
Clients who want a soothing extra with a manicure or pedicure.

blocks.note: Paraffin does not remove hair, lighten skin, cure infections or strengthen nails for good. Be honest with clients about what it does.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The consultation finds out whether the treatment is safe for this client today, and plans it to suit her. Do it in good light, with her hands or feet bare and clean enough to see.

flow: Explain the treatment and how it feels
Ask about her health and allergies
Examine the hands or feet closely
Decide: go ahead, adapt or refer
Agree the treatment and price
Record it and get her signature

head: Ask about
Why it matters
rows: Diabetes
Can reduce feeling and blood flow, so she may not feel heat and small injuries heal slowly. Needs her doctor's agreement; use the lower end of the safe temperature and watch closely.
Poor circulation; cold, pale or bluish hands or feet
Heat is harder for the skin to cope with, and sores heal slowly. Get medical advice first.
Loss of feeling (numbness), nerve damage, stroke
She cannot tell you if the wax is too hot, so she could be burned. Do not treat the numb area.
Heart conditions, high or low blood pressure
Heat can make her feel faint. Her doctor's agreement; shorter treatment; watch her.
Recent injury, operation, sprain or fracture
Heat increases swelling and bleeding. Wait until healed.
Skin conditions and infections
See the table below.
Allergies to wax, perfume, oils, lotions or latex
Choose an unscented wax and a plain cream; use vinyl or nitrile gloves.
Pregnancy
Not a reason to refuse, but keep the heat gentle and the session short, and stop if she feels unwell.
Very hairy skin
The wax can pull hairs as it comes off; a thin layer of cream first helps.

blocks.h: What to look for on the hands and feet

head: Condition
Contraindication?
What you do
rows: Open cuts, grazes, cracks that bleed, blisters
Yes
Do not apply wax. Wax and heat on broken skin cause pain and infection.
Burns, sunburn, red or inflamed skin
Yes
Do not add more heat. Wait until healed.
Rashes, eczema or dermatitis that is weeping or inflamed
Yes
Do not treat; suggest a doctor or pharmacist. Calm, unbroken dry patches can be treated gently with a plain cream.
Athlete's foot (tinea pedis): white, soggy, peeling, itchy skin between the toes
Yes, infectious
No foot treatment. Suggest a pharmacist or doctor.
Fungal nails: thick, yellow, crumbly
Yes, infectious
Do not treat; refer.
Verrucae and warts
Yes, infectious
Do not treat; refer.
Paronychia or any infected skin around a nail
Yes, infectious
Do not treat; refer.
Swelling, hot red areas, varicose veins that are painful
Yes
No heat; refer.
Corns, calluses and ingrown toenails
Not for the wax itself, but they need a podiatrist (chiropodist)
Wax can soften hard skin, but do not cut corns or dig at ingrown nails; refer.
Very dry or cracked skin that is not bleeding
No
This client benefits most. Cream first; gentle removal.

blocks.note: Feet carry more infections than hands. Before every foot treatment look between and under every toe, at the soles and heels, and at the corners of the big toenails, in good light. Wear gloves to handle feet with very hard or broken skin.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Do not name a disease. Describe what you have seen, kindly and in private, explain why the treatment cannot go ahead today, suggest a doctor, pharmacist or podiatrist, and record it. Then clean and disinfect everything the client touched.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Diabetes is common in Jamaica, and many clients who have it come for pedicures because they cannot reach their own feet. Ask every client, and ask a diabetic client whether her doctor or foot clinic is happy for her to have heat treatments. If she is unsure, give the manicure or pedicure without the wax.

head: Where to put the bath
Why
rows: On a stable trolley or table at the station, not on the floor
On the floor it can be kicked over, and the client would have to bend down over hot wax.
Away from the basin, foot spa and wet areas
Water and electricity; water splashed into hot wax spits.
Away from the edge, with the cable where no one walks
A pulled cable tips a bath of hot wax.
Where the client can reach it comfortably
She should not stretch or lean over it.

blocks.note: Jamaica's supply is 110 V (and 220 V for some heavy equipment) at 50 Hz. Check that the bath is made for the socket you plug it into, use a socket on its own rather than an overloaded adaptor, and keep a bath that holds litres of hot wax well away from any splash from the basin.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Clean towels; a plastic sheet or towel under the client's hands or feet to catch drips.
Liners, mitts or booties, brush, cleanser, cream, timer and record card within reach.
The lined, lidded bin close by.
For feet: a foot basin, foot cleanser and a comfortable chair with a footrest, so the feet can be raised.

blocks.p: Most harm from paraffin comes from wax that is too hot, from wet skin, or from a client who cannot feel heat. The thermostat does not make the treatment safe: **you** do, by testing every time.

flow: Check the bath's light or display shows it is ready
Read the thermometer if there is one
Stir the wax gently with a clean spatula or brush: the top can be hotter than the rest
Dab a little wax on the inside of your own wrist
If it feels comfortable, dab a little on a small area of the client's skin
Ask her how it feels before any more goes on
Too hot? Turn the thermostat down, wait, and test again

head: Rule
Why
rows: Test on the **inside of your wrist**, not your fingers
The skin there is thin and sensitive, like the client's. Fingers that work with heat all day feel less.
Then test on the client
Her skin may be more sensitive than yours, and she must agree it is comfortable.
Test before **every** client, even in a busy day
The thermostat can drift, the wax level changes, and someone may have turned the dial.
Skin must be completely dry
Water on the skin heats up under the wax and can scald; water in the bath spits and spoils the wax.
Never guess from the look of the wax
Clear, runny wax may be far hotter than it looks.
Do not ask the client to test it by dipping
She could be burned before she can pull away.

blocks.note: Lower the temperature, shorten the treatment and watch even more closely for clients who feel heat less well: older clients, diabetic clients and those with poor circulation. If in doubt, do not treat.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Giving the treatment: hands and feet

blocks.h: Three ways to apply the wax

head: Method
How
Best for
Hygiene
rows: Dip
The hand is dipped into the bath several times.
Hands; a bath big enough for feet.
The client's skin touches the shared wax, so the hands must be cleansed first. Many salons use it only for hands.
Brush
Warm wax is painted on in layers with a clean brush.
Feet, elbows, knees and any area that cannot be dipped; clients whose hands should not go into the bath.
The brush, not the client, touches the bath. Each client's wax is only the wax on her skin.
Portion in a liner
A portion of melted wax is poured into a disposable liner bag or bowl for that client; the hand or foot goes into the liner, or the wax is spread over the skin inside it.
Feet; the most hygienic choice for every client.
The client never touches the main bath; the liner and wax are thrown away.

blocks.h: Hand treatment by the dip method

flow: Consult, check for contraindications, complete the record card
Wash your hands; the client removes rings, bracelets and watch
Cleanse her hands with an antibacterial product and dry them completely
Apply hand cream or treatment lotion
Test the wax on your inner wrist, then on a small area of her skin
She spreads her fingers slightly and dips one hand to the wrist, without touching the bottom or sides, then lifts it out and holds it still a few seconds
Dip again: about three to five dips in all, each slightly lower than the last so the edge stays even
Slip the hand into a plastic liner, then a thermal mitt or wrap it in a towel
Repeat for the other hand
Start the timer: about 10 to 15 minutes, as the maker says
Remove the mitt and liner; peel the wax off from the wrist towards the fingers, in one piece if you can
Put the wax and liner in the bin
Massage the remaining cream into the hands and lower arms

head: Point of method
Why
rows: Rings and bracelets off
Metal heats up and wax gets caught under them.
Fingers slightly apart
Wax reaches between the fingers and the layer is even; fingers pressed together stick and tear the coat.
Do not touch the bottom or sides of the bath
The metal is hotter than the wax and can burn.
Hold the hand still between dips
Moving cracks the layer, lets heat out and makes it messy.
Several thin dips, not one long dip
Each layer sets a little, building a thick, even coat that holds the heat; one long dip is a burn risk.
Liner, then mitt
The liner keeps the heat and moisture in and keeps the mitt clean.
Peel from wrist to fingers
Follows the shape of the hand and comes off in one piece.
Used wax in the bin
It carries dead skin, sweat, cream and germs, and would contaminate the bath.

blocks.h: Foot treatment by the brush or liner method

flow: Consult; check between and under the toes, the soles and the nail corners
Cleanse the feet, or soak and dry them in a pedicure; dry well between the toes
Apply foot cream
Test the wax on your inner wrist, then on a small area of the foot
Brush the wax on quickly in even layers, several coats, or pour a portion into a disposable foot liner and place the foot in it
Wrap each foot in a liner and a thermal bootie or towel
Raise the feet on a footrest so she is comfortable
Time the treatment: about 10 to 15 minutes, as the maker says
Remove from the ankle downwards and throw the wax away
Massage in the cream; cleanse the nails if polish is to follow

blocks.note: A foot should never go into a hand-sized bath, and a client should never stand in a bath. If the bath is too small or you are not sure the foot can go in safely, brush the wax on or use a portion in a liner.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Where paraffin fits in a manicure or pedicure

head: Step
Manicure
Pedicure
rows: Consultation; remove old polish
Consultation; remove old polish; foot soak
File and shape; cuticle work
Dry the feet; file and shape; cuticle work; hard skin smoothed
Cleanse and **dry** the hands; apply cream
Cleanse and **dry** the feet; apply cream
**Paraffin wax**: apply, wrap, time, remove
**Paraffin wax**: brush or liner method, wrap, time, remove
Massage in the cream
Foot and leg massage
Wipe the nail plates with remover; base coat, colour, top coat
Wipe the nail plates with remover; polish

ul: Paraffin comes **after** cleaning and nail work, so the wax goes on clean skin and softened cuticles, and the heat does not spoil work already done.
It comes **before** the polish: the wax and cream leave oil on the nail plates, and polish will not stick to oil. Wipe the plates with remover before the base coat.
Polish applied before wax would be smudged and dulled by the heat and the oils.
A client can also have paraffin on its own, after cleansing, as a short treatment.

blocks.note: Wax that gets on the floor sets slippery and hard. Let a spill cool and set, then scrape and peel it up; do not try to mop it while it is liquid. Keep paper or a towel under the client's hands to catch drips.
blocks.label: Tip

head: What happens
Cause
What you do
rows: Skin slightly pink and warm
Normal: more blood flowing to the skin.
Nothing; tell her it will fade soon.
Burning or stinging as the wax goes on
Wax too hot; skin wet; client feels heat poorly.
Remove the wax **at once** and cool the skin under cool running water. Check the thermostat before any other client.
A red, painful burn, perhaps with a blister
As above.

Cool under cool running water for about 20 minutes. Do not put butter, cream, toothpaste or ice on it; do not burst blisters. Cover loosely with a clean, non-fluffy dressing. Get a first aider; medical help for a large burn or one on a diabetic client. Record and report it.
Itching, rash, blotches or swelling
Allergy or sensitivity to the wax, the scent, the oils or the cream.
Stop; remove the product; rinse with cool water; apply a cool compress. Advise a doctor or pharmacist if it does not settle. Record which products were used and do not use them on her again.
Feeling faint, dizzy, sick or very hot
Heat; low blood pressure; low blood sugar in a diabetic client.
Stop; remove the mitts or booties; sit her comfortably with the feet up if she is faint; give water; fresh air. Get help if she does not recover quickly.
Wax pulling hairs or sticking
Hairy skin; too little cream.
Peel slowly in the direction of hair growth; use more cream next time.

blocks.note: Every contra-action is written on the record card and reported to your supervisor, even a small one. The next therapist needs to know, and the salon needs to find the cause.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Wash your hands before and after every client.
Cleanse the client's hands or feet with an antibacterial product before any wax is applied: germs on the skin would otherwise go into the wax.
Never treat broken, infected or inflamed skin.
Prefer the brush or liner method, so the client's skin does not touch the main bath; always for feet.
**Used wax is never returned to the bath.** It carries dead skin cells, sweat, hairs, cream and germs that would pass to the next client. It goes in the lined, lidded bin.
A new liner for every client; mitts and booties cleaned as the maker says, with a liner always between the wax and the mitt.
Keep the lid on the bath when it is not in use, to keep out dust, hair and insects and to hold the heat in.
Clean the bath and change the wax as often as the maker says, and sooner if it looks dirty or has been contaminated.
Clean and disinfect foot basins, the trolley and the chair after each client; towels to the laundry.

blocks.note: The word for germs passing from one person or object to another is **cross-infection**. In this treatment the shared bath, the mitts, the brush and the foot basin are the places it happens. Each has its own control: cleanse, liner, new or clean brush, disinfect.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Fire, electrical safety and care of the bath

ul: Paraffin wax is flammable. Overheated wax smokes, then catches fire. Melt it **only** in a paraffin bath with a working thermostat, never in a pot on a gas stove, in a microwave or over a flame.
Keep the bath away from naked flames, candles, heaters and sunlight, and keep aerosols and alcohol-based products away from it.
Fill only to the maker's line, so the wax does not spill onto the heating element.
Never leave the bath switched on unattended, and never overnight. Switch off and unplug at the end of the day.

If wax catches fire, do not use water: it spreads burning wax. Switch off at the socket if it is safe, smother the flames with the lid or a fire blanket, and raise the alarm. Use the extinguisher the salon has for electrical and liquid fires (such as CO2 or dry powder) if you are trained.
Check the plug, cable and casing before each use. A cracked plug, a split cable or wax on the connections means do not use it: label it and report it.
Dry hands when you touch the plug and switch.
No water near the bath; no bath near the basin or foot spa.
Do not move the bath while the wax is liquid. Let it cool, or move it with great care on a trolley.
Repairs are for a qualified person, as the salon arranges.

flow: Switch off and unplug
Let the wax cool and set, or let the bath cool with the wax liquid, as the maker says
Lift out the set wax block, or pour out the liquid wax as the maker directs, if the wax is being changed
Wipe the inside with paper towel; clean with the cleaner the maker allows when the bath is cool
Wipe the outside; check the cable
Refill with fresh wax and keep the lid on
Store covered, in a dry place

blocks.note: Never pour liquid wax down the sink: it sets in the pipes. Let it set in a liner or on paper and put it in the general waste, following the local rules.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: Follow the bath's instructions for how often to change the wax. Many makers suggest after a set number of uses or when the wax looks dirty; some salons change it weekly in a busy season. Write the date of each change on a log.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Advice
Why
rows: Avoid very hot water, harsh soaps and detergents for the rest of the day
The skin is warm, soft and freshly moisturised; heat and detergent would undo the work.
Apply hand or foot cream every day, especially after washing
Keeps the moisture the treatment put in.
Wear gloves for washing clothes, cleaning, gardening and farm work
Protects the skin from water, detergent, soil and cement.
Use sunscreen on the hands and feet in the sun
Jamaica's sun dries, darkens and ages the skin.
Dry well between the toes; clean, dry socks; well-fitting shoes
Prevents fungal infection and cracked skin.
Do not pick at dry skin or cuticles
Keeps the skin's barrier whole.
If redness, itching or soreness appears later, contact the salon; see a doctor if it does not settle
A late reaction must be recorded and may need treatment.
Come back regularly: for example every few weeks with a manicure or pedicure
The benefit builds up with regular treatment.

blocks.p: Suggest the hand or foot cream you used, and tell the client how and when to use it. Be honest, give the price clearly in J$, and never pressure her. Record what she buys.

blocks.note: The temperature test and the client's reaction go on the card so that the next therapist can treat her safely: she knows what this client found comfortable and what, if anything, went wrong. Cards are personal information and are kept private and secure under Jamaica's Data Protection Act.

c1.title: A busy afternoon in Santa Cruz
c1.text: At a salon in Santa Cruz, trainee Latoya has three paraffin hand treatments booked one after another. She tested the wax on her wrist for the first client at 1 p.m. It is now 2:30 p.m.; the thermostat light shows the bath is ready, and her third client, Mrs. Beverley Scott, 67, who has arthritis in her fingers and 'cold hands', is waiting. Latoya is about to ask Mrs. Scott to dip her hand straight in. Mrs. Scott's hands have just been soaked and are still damp.

c2.title: A cane cutter's feet in Frome
c2.text: Mr. Winston Campbell, 54, cuts cane near Frome and wears rubber boots all day. His wife has booked him a pedicure with paraffin wax for his cracked heels. Trainee Deneika finds the heels dry and very hard, with one deep crack that is bleeding slightly. The skin between his toes is dry but not peeling, and his toenails look normal. The salon has only a hand-sized paraffin bath.

c3.title: Burning in Ocho Rios
c3.text: At a hotel spa in Ocho Rios, a visitor, Mrs. Angela Reid, says her left hand is burning a few seconds after her first dip. Trainee Jerome tells her the feeling will soon pass and dips the hand a second time. When he finally removes the wax, the back of her hand is red and a small blister has formed. Another therapist suggests rubbing aloe gel and butter on it. Later, Jerome's supervisor finds the thermostat dial turned to its highest setting.

c4.title: Saving wax in May Pen
c4.text: A small salon in May Pen is trying to cut costs. The owner's niece, trainee Shanique, is told by another staff member to melt the peeled-off wax back into the bath so that it lasts longer, to leave the bath switched on overnight so it is ready in the morning, and to skip the antibacterial cleanse 'because the wax is hot enough to kill germs'. The bath stands on the edge of the shampoo basin counter, with its cable across the walkway.

c5.title: A pedicure with polish in Brown's Town
c5.text: Miss Tamara Ellis, 31, a nurse in Brown's Town, has a pedicure with a paraffin foot treatment and red polish. Trainee Kadeem has already filed and shaped the nails and smoothed the hard skin. He wonders whether to polish the toenails first so that they dry while the wax is on. Tamara mentions that scented lotions sometimes make her skin itch.

questions.q: Latoya tested the wax for her first client at 1 p.m. What should she do before Mrs. Scott's hands go in?
o: Dip straight away, as the thermostat light shows the wax is ready
Ask Mrs. Scott to dip one fingertip in quickly to check the heat
Test again on her own inner wrist, then on Mrs. Scott's skin
Look at the wax: if it is clear and runny the temperature is right
questions.why: The wax is tested before every client, not once a day: the thermostat can drift, the level changes and the dial may have been moved. The therapist's wrist first, then a small area of the client's skin, and the client's agreement.

questions.q: Mrs. Scott's hands are still damp from the soak. Why does that matter?
o: Damp skin stops the wax from sticking, so the layer falls off
Water heats up under the wax and can scald, and spoils the bath
Water cools the wax so much that it will not hold any heat
Damp hands turn the paraffin cloudy and make it set too quickly
questions.why: Water trapped between hot wax and skin heats up and can burn, and water in the bath makes the wax spit and spoils it. The hands must be completely dry before any wax goes on.

questions.q: Mrs. Scott's 'cold hands' and arthritis mean Latoya should take which extra care?
o: Turn the thermostat up, so the warmth can reach her stiff joints
Leave the wax on for 40 minutes, as older joints need longer heat
Use a lower setting, a shorter time, and watch her closely
Refuse the treatment, as arthritis is always a contraindication
questions.why: Cold hands suggest poor circulation, and an older client may feel heat less well, so burns are more likely. Arthritis is a reason the treatment helps, with her doctor's agreement, but the heat must be gentle and she must be watched.

questions.q: Mrs. Scott asks how many times she should dip. What should Latoya say?
o: Once, held in the wax for about a minute to build a thick coat
About three to five times, holding the hand still between dips
At least ten times, as quickly as she can, to keep the heat in
As many times as she likes, until the wax feels heavy on the hand
questions.why: Several short dips, each setting a little before the next, build an even coat that holds the heat. One long dip is a burn risk, and too many dips make a thick, cracking layer.

questions.q: What should Deneika do about Mr. Campbell's heels?
o: Wax both feet as booked; the warmth will heal the crack faster
Cover the crack with polish to seal it, then wax both feet
Not wax the foot with the bleeding crack; suggest he sees a doctor
Scrape the hard skin off with a blade first, then wax both feet
questions.why: Broken, bleeding skin is a contraindication: hot wax on it causes pain and infection. The other foot can be treated if it is sound, and a deep crack and such hard skin are best seen by a doctor or podiatrist. Never cut hard skin with a blade.

questions.q: The salon has only a hand-sized bath. How should the wax be applied to a foot that can be treated?
o: Ask Mr. Campbell to press his foot into the bath as far as it fits
Brush the wax on in even layers, or use a portion in a foot liner
Pour the wax from the bath over his foot while it rests in a basin
Skip the wax and soak the foot in very hot water for longer instead
questions.why: A foot never goes into a bath too small for it, and wax is never poured from a height onto skin. The brush method or a portion of wax in a disposable liner gives an even, hygienic layer on any area that cannot be dipped.

questions.q: Which aftercare advice matters most for Mr. Campbell's feet?
o: Dry well between the toes, cream daily, clean socks
Soak the feet in hot water each night to keep the heels soft
Wear the boots without socks so that the feet stay cooler
Scrape the hard skin off at home with a razor blade once a week
questions.why: Rubber boots keep the feet warm and damp, which breeds fungal infection and dries and cracks the skin. Drying between the toes, daily cream and clean socks keep the benefit of the treatment; hot soaks and blades do harm.

questions.q: What should Jerome have done the moment Mrs. Reid said the wax was burning?
o: Dipped the hand again, as a second layer cools the first
Wrapped the hand quickly in a mitt to hold the heat evenly
Removed the wax at once and cooled the skin with cool water
Told her to wait, as the first dip always feels hot for a while
questions.why: Burning is not normal: it means the wax is too hot or the skin was wet. Remove the wax immediately and cool the skin under cool running water, then check the thermostat before anyone else is treated.

questions.q: Which first aid is right for the blister on Mrs. Reid's hand?
o: Rub in aloe gel and butter, then cover it with a plaster
Cool it under running water; do not burst it; cover loosely
Burst the blister with a clean pin so the fluid can drain
Put ice straight on the blister for ten minutes
questions.why: A burn is cooled under cool running water for about 20 minutes and covered loosely with a clean, non-fluffy dressing. Butter, gels, creams and ice can damage the skin further, and a burst blister lets infection in. The burn is recorded and reported.

questions.q: Apart from first aid, what must happen after Mrs. Reid's burn?
o: Nothing more, as long as she accepts an apology and a discount
Record it, report it, and check the thermostat
Throw away the bath and buy a new one before the next client
Ask Mrs. Reid to sign a form saying the burn was her own fault
questions.why: Every contra-action is written on the record card and in the salon's accident record and reported, so that the cause is found. Here the dial had been turned up: the thermostat must be reset and the wax tested before the next client.

questions.q: Why must the peeled-off wax never be melted back into the bath?
o: It has lost its oils, so it would make the fresh wax too hard
It sets at a higher temperature, so the bath would overheat
It carries dead skin, sweat and germs to other clients
It has absorbed water, so the wax would never melt again
questions.why: Wax that has been on a client's skin is contaminated with skin cells, sweat, cream and germs. Putting it back would spread them to every later client. Used wax and liners go in the lined, lidded bin.

questions.q: What is wrong with leaving the bath switched on overnight?
o: The wax will go cloudy and lose its scent by the morning
An unattended heater of flammable wax is a fire risk
The thermostat will wear out after a few nights of use
The bath will be too hot to switch off in the morning
questions.why: Paraffin is flammable and the bath is an electric heater. If the thermostat fails or the unit faults with nobody there, the wax can overheat and catch fire. Switch off and unplug at the end of the day and melt the wax in good time in the morning.

questions.q: Is it true that the hot wax makes the antibacterial cleanse unnecessary?
o: Yes: paraffin is held well above the temperature that kills germs
Yes, as long as the client dips only once and very quickly
No: the wax is too cool to kill germs, so skin is cleansed
No: the cleanse is only needed so that the wax sticks to the skin
questions.why: The bath is kept at a comfortable warm temperature, far below what would kill germs, and the dip puts the client's skin into a product shared by every client. Cleansing the skin first protects the bath and the next client.

questions.q: Where should the bath be moved to?
o: Onto the floor beside the chair, where it cannot fall off anything
Onto a stable trolley away from water, cable clear of the walkway
Onto the counter but turned so the cable runs behind the basin taps
Onto a high shelf, so that nobody can knock it during the day
questions.why: A bath of hot wax belongs on a stable, level surface where it cannot be knocked, away from water, with its cable tidy. On the counter edge by the basin it risks water, splashes and a pulled cable; on the floor it can be kicked and the client must bend over it.

questions.q: Should Kadeem polish Tamara's toenails before the paraffin?
o: Yes: the warm wax will set the polish harder and faster
Yes: polishing first keeps the wax off the nail plates
No: the heat and oils would spoil it, and polish comes last
No: polish should be applied before the nails are shaped
questions.why: Paraffin and cream leave oil on the nails and the heat would smudge and dull fresh polish. Wax comes after cleaning and nail work and before polish; the plates are wiped with remover, then the polish goes on last.

questions.q: Tamara says scented lotions sometimes make her skin itch. What should Kadeem do?
o: Use the usual scented wax and lotion, but leave the wax on for less time
Use an unscented wax and a plain cream, and record her sensitivity
Cancel the paraffin treatment, as any sensitivity rules out heat
Use the scented wax but no cream at all, so there is less to react to
questions.why: An itchy reaction to scent is a sensitivity, not a reason to refuse the treatment. Choose plain, unscented products, watch for a reaction, and write it on her card so the next therapist knows.

questions.q: After the wax comes off, what should Kadeem do before applying the base coat?
o: Soak the feet again so the polish goes on to damp nails
Massage in the cream, then wipe the nail plates with remover
Apply the base coat straight away while the nails are still warm
File the nails again to remove the layer of wax from them
questions.why: The remaining cream is massaged in as part of the treatment, and then the oily film on the nail plates is removed with remover, because polish will not stick to oil. Nails were shaped before the wax; they do not need filing again.

questions.q: A client's hands are pink and feel warm when the wax comes off. What does this show?
o: A mild burn that needs cool water at once
An allergy to the oils in the wax
The normal increase in blood flow from the heat
The wax was too cool to have any effect
questions.why: Warmth widens the small blood vessels in the skin, so slight pinkness and warmth are normal and fade soon. A burn is painful; an allergy itches or comes up in blotches or swelling.

questions.q: Why is a plastic liner put between the wax and the thermal mitt?
o: It holds in heat and moisture and keeps the mitt clean
It cools the wax quickly so that it can be peeled off sooner
It stops the wax from sticking to the client's skin at all
It makes the mitt waterproof so it never needs cleaning
questions.why: The liner keeps the warmth and moisture against the skin and stops wax and cream getting on the mitt, which is shared between clients. The mitt is still cleaned as the maker says.

questions.q: Which client could have a paraffin hand treatment today?
o: A client with a weeping rash across both palms
A client whose fingertips went numb after a stroke
A client with rough, dry hands from washing clothes
A client with a fresh burn on the back of her hand
questions.why: Dry, rough, hard-working hands are exactly what the treatment helps. A weeping rash and a fresh burn are broken or inflamed skin, and numb fingertips cannot warn of heat, so those clients are not treated.
